a OurBigBook.com
The image of a function f:A→B is
f(A)={f(a):a∈A}⊆B.​
(1)
The function is surjective, or onto, exactly when every b∈B equals f(a) for at least one a∈A, equivalently f(A)=B. It is injective, or one-to-one, exactly when
∀a,a′∈A,f(a)=f(a′)⟹a=a′.​
(2)
Thus surjectivity concerns whether the entire codomain is reached; injectivity concerns whether distinct inputs have distinct outputs.

Words: 59
i OurBigBook.com
Since x2+1≥2∣x∣, the image of a function is contained in [−1/2,1/2]. Both endpoints occur, at x=−1 and x=1. By continuity and the intermediate value theorem applied on [−1,1], every intermediate value occurs too. Hence
f(R)=[−1/2,1/2],f is neither onto nor one-to-one.​
(3)
It is not surjective onto R because, for example, 1 is not attained. It is not injective because f(2)=f(1/2)=2/5 although 2=1/2.

If 0≤x<y, then x​<y​ and x<y, so x​+x<y​+y. Thus the function is strictly increasing on its domain and is injective. Its values are nonnegative, so it is not surjective onto R:
one-to-one, but not onto.​
(4)
If R+​ means (0,∞) its image of a function is (0,∞); if it includes zero its image of a function is [0,∞). Indeed, for any u>0, set t=(1+4u​−1)/2>0 and x=t2; then x​+x=t+t2=u. This convention does not change the classification.

Solution
Words: 98
iii OurBigBook.com
With the convention N={0,1,2,…}, the even inputs 2j map to j for j≥0, while the odd inputs 2j+1 map to −(j+1) for j≥0. These two images of a function are disjoint and together equal Z. Within either class there are no repeated outputs. More explicitly the inverse function is
f−1(z)={2z,−2z−1,​z≥0,z<0.​​
(5)
Consequently f is both injective and surjective, hence a bijection. If instead N={1,2,…}, the input zero is absent: f remains injective but its image of a function is Z∖{0}, so it is not onto. The printed paper does not specify this convention; the zero-based convention gives the apparent intended bijection.

For every set S, the definition of a power set gives
S∈P(A∩B)​⟺S⊆A∩B⟺(S⊆A and S⊆B)⟺S∈P(A)∩P(B).​
(9)
Equality by identical membership therefore proves
P(A∩B)=P(A)∩P(B).​
(10)
The essential observation is that being a subset of a set intersection means being a subset of both factors.

ii

Words: 134 Articles: 1
d OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 134
ii OurBigBook.com
First suppose the sets are finite, with cardinalities a=∣A∣≥2 and b=∣B∣≥2. The power set and Cartesian product counting rules give
∣P(A×B)∣=2ab,∣P(A)×P(B)∣=2a+b.
(11)
Since ab−a−b=(a−1)(b−1)−1≥0, the desired inequality follows.
The power-set product cardinality inequality also has an injection proof that does not assume finiteness. Choose distinct a0​,a1​∈A and distinct b0​,b1​∈B. For S⊆A and T⊆B, define the subset of A×B
Φ(S,T)=(S×{b0​})∪({a0​}×(T∖{b0​}))∪ET​,ET​={{(a1​,b1​)},∅,​b0​∈T,b0​∈/T.​
(12)
These three encoding regions are disjoint. The row with second coordinate b0​ recovers S; the column with first coordinate a0​ and second coordinate different from b0​ recovers T∖{b0​}; the extra position (a1​,b1​) records whether b0​∈T. Thus Φ is injective, proving for arbitrary sets
∣P(A×B)∣≥∣P(A)×P(B)∣.​
(13)
Encoding by S×T alone would fail: all pairs with either factor empty would have the same output.

(k−1n+k−1​)​(k≥1).

The initial values of the two sequences agree: c0​=d0​=1 and c1​=−1+c0​=0=d1​. For n≥2, use the first-order recurrence relation at n and n−1:
cn​−(n−1)(cn−1​+cn−2​)​=(−1)n+cn−1​−(n−1)cn−2​=(−1)n+(−1)n−1=0.​
(21)
Therefore cn​ satisfies exactly the same derangement recurrence as dn​. By strong induction, equality of the preceding two terms implies equality of the next term. Consequently
cn​=dn​for every n≥0.​
(22)
The first-order recurrence relation therefore also counts derangements.

For a binary relation R⊆A×A, reflexivity means aRa for every a∈A; a symmetric relation satisfies aRb⇒bRa for every a,b∈A; an antisymmetric relation satisfies (aRb and bRa)⇒a=b for every a,b∈A; transitivity means (aRb and bRc)⇒aRc for every a,b,c∈A; an irreflexive relation satisfies ¬(aRa) for every a∈A. In particular, failure of reflexivity means at least one missing diagonal pair, whereas irreflexivity requires every diagonal pair to be missing.

There are n2 possible ordered pairs and hence 2n2 binary relations. A reflexive relation must contain the n diagonal pairs, while its remaining n2−n pairs are unrestricted. Subtracting the reflexive relations gives
2n2−2n2−n​
(23)
binary relations that are not reflexive.

A symmetric relation has n independent choices on the diagonal. For each of the (2n​) unordered pairs {a,b} of distinct elements, either both ordered pairs are included or neither is. Thus there are 2n+(2n​) symmetric relations, so the requested number is
2n2−2n+(2n​)=2n2−2n(n+1)/2.​
(24)

iii

Words: 66 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 66
iii OurBigBook.com
For each unordered pair {a,b} with a=b, antisymmetry allows three choices: neither direction, only (a,b), or only (b,a). This contributes 3(2n​). The diagonal is unrestricted by antisymmetry, but being not irreflexive requires a nonempty subset of the n diagonal pairs. There are 2n−1 such choices. Hence
(2n−1)3(2n​).​
(25)
This allows some diagonal pairs to be absent; “not irreflexive” does not require a reflexive relation.

We prove the stronger bound T(n)≤2n2 for every n≥1 by strong induction. The initial case is T(1)=1≤2. For n≥2, put m=⌊n/2⌋. Then 1≤m<n, so the induction hypothesis and the defining recurrence relation give

The recurrence relation must be read as applying for n≥2; applying it at n=1 would invoke T(0) outside the printed domain. No value of T(0) is needed.

r=a−qn≡b−sn=t(modn).

r=t,​

For y=1+x2, the derivatives are y′=2x and y′′=2. Its endpoint values are y(0)=1 and y(2)=5, so it satisfies both the ordinary differential equation and the boundary conditions. Moreover any solution of y′′=2 has the form x2+Ax+B; the boundary conditions force B=1 and A=0. Thus the unique solution of the boundary value problem is
y(x)=1+x2.​

The endpoint boundary conditions are
y0​=1,yN​=5.​
(52)
The finite difference equation can be written yn+1​−2yn​+yn−1​=2h2. Set dn​=yn​−yn−1​. Then dn+1​−dn​=2h2, so dn​=d1​+2h2(n−1). Summing from 1 to n gives
yn​=1+nd1​+h2n(n−1).
(53)
Using yN​=5 and h=2/N yields Nd1​=4−h2N(N−1)=4/N, hence d1​=4/N2=h2. Therefore
yn​=1+h2n2=1+(N2n​)2=y(xn​),0≤n≤N.​
(54)
This also covers N=1, where there are no interior equations. Uniqueness follows because the difference of two solutions has zero second finite difference, hence is linear in n, and vanishes at both endpoints. This is an exact finite difference solution for constant second derivative: the method is exact at the nodes here because the centered second finite difference differentiates this quadratic polynomial exactly.

For Lagrange multipliers λ,μ, the stationarity equation ∇f=λ∇g1​+μ∇g2​ becomes

There are no missing singular constraint points: on the feasible circle, the two constraint gradients (3,2y,2z) and (−3,2y,2z) are linearly independent, since y2+z2=7/4>0. Thus the complete list of constrained critical points and critical values is
(x,y,z)=(23​,±27​​,0),f=±27​​.​
(66)
The bound ∣y∣≤7​/2 on the feasible circle shows that the positive value is the global maximum and the negative value is the global minimum.

At x=0, g′′(0)=36>0, so the second-derivative test gives a strict local minimum. In fact g′(x)=4x(x−3)2 is negative for x<0 and positive for x>0 except at x=3, so g(0)=5 is the global minimum as well.
At x=3, the second-derivative test is inconclusive because g′′(3)=0. But g′′(x)=12(x−1)(x−3) changes from negative to positive across 3, while g′(3)=0. Hence this is a stationary inflection point. Equivalently, the leading nonconstant term 4(x−3)3 in the Taylor polynomial changes sign across 3. The paper explicitly uses “saddle point” to mean an inflection point, so in its terminology the classification is
x=0: minimum;x=3: saddle point;no maxima.​
(77)
Here the “saddle point” is a one-dimensional stationary inflection point, rather than the usual multivariable use of saddle point of a scalar function.[ref]

To obtain the (k+1)st head on toss n+1, the first n tosses must contain exactly k heads, and the last toss must be a head. There are (kn​) choices of the first k head positions. By independence, each such arrangement followed by a head has probability rk(1−r)n−kr. The arrangements are disjoint, so
hn,k​(r)=(kn​)(1−r)n−krk+1,n≥k≥0.​
(80)
This is the negative binomial stopping argument, with n+1 counting all tosses up to and including the (k+1)st success. It is not merely the probability of k+1 heads somewhere among n+1 tosses: the last toss is prescribed to be a head.

This illustrates Bernoulli thinning of a geometric count. Here 0<p∗​<1, as 0<p,q<1.

GM​(u)=∑m=0∞​e−λm!λm​um=eλ(u−1).

For each student, the probability of both falling asleep and dreaming about mathematics is (1−p)q. These indicators are independent across students, so the same Poisson thinning calculation gives, for the requested count D,
D∼Poisson(λ(1−p)q).​

Explicitly GD​(s)=exp(λ(1−p)q(s−1)), the probability generating function of that Poisson distribution.

Given M=m, there are exactly m independent opportunities to stay awake, each with probability p. Hence
W∣M=m∼Binomial(m,p).​
(97)
The standard binomial distribution formulas are E[W∣M]=pM and var(W∣M)=Mp(1−p). The Poisson distribution formulas are E[M]=λ, var(M)=λ, and therefore E[M2]=λ2+λ. By the law of total expectation,
E[WM]=E[ME[W∣M]]=pE[M2]=p(λ2+λ),E[W]=pλ.
(98)
Using the definition of covariance,
cov(W,M)=E[WM]−E[W]E[M]=pλ.​
(99)
Thus W and M are not independent, even though the separate awake and asleep counts produced by Poisson thinning are independent.
